title: How to Find Teaming Partners for Government Contracts
summary: Where primes and subcontractors find each other, and how to vet a partner before you sign.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** The best places to find teaming partners for government contracts are award data (who already holds the work and who they subcontract to), SBA's subcontracting and small business search tools, and the holder lists of the contract vehicles you want to reach. Find partners who fill a specific gap, such as a vehicle, a set-aside status, a capability or past performance, then vet them and put the workshare in writing before the solicitation drops.


‍


## What is a teaming arrangement in government contracting?


A teaming arrangement is an agreement between companies to pursue a government contract together. The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) has long described two forms in[FAR Subpart 9.6](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/subpart-9.6) : two or more companies forming a partnership or joint venture to act as the prime contractor, or a prime contractor agreeing with other companies to act as its subcontractors on a specific program. In both cases the government holds the prime fully responsible for performance.


One update to know: the 2025 FAR overhaul's[model text for Part 9](https://www.acquisition.gov/far-overhaul/far-part-deviation-guide/far-overhaul-part-9) drops Subpart 9.6, and agencies adopting it treat that guidance as non-regulatory. Teaming itself hasn't gone anywhere. Solicitations still commonly ask offerors to name their team, so read each one for its own rules.


Small businesses have one more structure. Under SBA's[Mentor-Protégé Program](https://www.sba.gov/mpp) , a mentor and protégé can form a joint venture that competes as a small business for set-aside contracts the protégé qualifies for.


‍


## Where do primes and subcontractors find each other?


Most strong partnerships start from evidence of who already does the work. These are the main sources:


- **Award data.** Prime awards show who holds the work today. Subaward records show who those primes subcontract to.
- **SBA SubNet.**[SubNet](https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-guide/prime-subcontracting/subcontracting-opportunities) is SBA's listing of subcontracting opportunities from large primes looking for small subcontractors. Questions go to each posting's contact, not to SBA.
- **SBA Small Business Search.** The successor to SBA's Dynamic Small Business Search (DSBS),[Small Business Search](https://search.certifications.sba.gov/) lets primes look up small firms by capability and certification.
- **SAM.gov entity search.**[SAM.gov](https://sam.gov/content/entity-information) lets you look up registered entities and check that a potential partner's registration is active.
- **Contract vehicle holder lists.** If you need access to a governmentwide acquisition contract (GWAC) or indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity (IDIQ) contract you don't hold, the holder list is your shortlist.
- **Industry days and sources sought.** Attendee lists and responses show who is chasing the same requirement.


‍


## How do you use award data to pick a partner?


Start with the specific opportunity, not a general networking list.


1. **Find the incumbent.** Pull the current or predecessor contract and its task orders. Our guide on[how to find the incumbent on a government contract](https://www.govly.com/blog/find-incumbent-government-contract) walks through it.
2. **Look below the prime.** Primes report first-tier subawards, now in SAM.gov after[FSRS.gov retired in March 2025](https://sam.gov/alerts/subaward-reporting-live-samgov) , and the data appears on[USAspending.gov](https://www.usaspending.gov/) . The reporting rule covers contracts of $40,000 or more under[FAR subpart 4.14](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/4.1403) . Expect some duplicate records.
3. **Check who needs small business help.** Under[FAR Part 19](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/19.702) , other-than-small primes generally need a small business subcontracting plan on contracts expected to exceed $900,000 ($2 million for construction). Those primes have a reason to take your call.
4. **Map the vehicle.** If the work flows through a contract vehicle, much of it never shows up on SAM.gov, as we explain in[why contract vehicle RFQs don't appear on SAM.gov](https://www.govly.com/blog/contract-vehicle-rfqs-not-on-sam-gov) . The partner you need may simply be a holder.


‍


## When does teaming make the most sense?


Teaming works best when each company brings something the other can't get quickly:


- **Vehicle access.** You have the product or service; they hold the contract.
- **Set-aside eligibility.** A small or certified firm leads, and a larger partner adds scale.
- **Capability or past performance gaps.** One partner covers a technical area or brings relevant past performance the evaluation rewards.
- **Recompetes.** Joining, or unseating, an incumbent team is often easier than bidding alone against it.


Rules on how teams can bid vary by procurement and can change mid-stream. In October, the Army[reopened its $50 billion MAPS contract](https://www.washingtontechnology.com/contracts/2026/10/army-reopens-50b-maps-contract-small-business-teams-only/416593/) so small business teaming arrangements could compete, not just small business joint ventures. Read each solicitation's teaming language before you commit.


‍


## What should you check before you sign a teaming agreement?


Vet partners like you'd vet a hire. Use this checklist:


- Confirm their SAM.gov registration is active and their size and certifications match what the solicitation needs.
- Verify past performance in award data, not just on their capability statement.
- Confirm which vehicles they hold and whether they are in the right category or pool for this work.
- Ask about security requirements, such as clearances or Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) status, if the work involves controlled information.
- Agree on workshare, ideally by task or labor category, and how it changes if the scope changes.
- Decide on exclusivity: whether either side can join another team on the same bid.
- Set rules for sharing proposal content, pricing and customer contacts, usually with a nondisclosure agreement.
- Spell out what happens after award, including when the subcontract will be signed and on what terms.
- Have counsel review size and affiliation questions, especially for joint ventures and set-asides.

## FAQ


**Is a teaming agreement legally binding?**
It depends on its terms and the governing state law. Agreements that leave the future subcontract's terms open are harder to enforce, so have counsel review yours.


**Can you team with a company you compete against?**
Yes. Companies that compete on one pursuit often team on another, and the exclusivity clause decides whether you can do both on the same bid.


**How early should you start looking for partners?**
Ideally before the final solicitation. Once an RFP is out, the strongest partners are often already committed to other teams.


**Does a subcontractor need to hold the contract vehicle?**
No. On most vehicles only the prime holds the contract, though the order can pass requirements such as security clauses down to subcontractors.
